title: Rethinking the Gut-Bone Axis: Diet, the Gut Ecosystem, and Skeletal Health.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: The gut-bone field has expanded beyond its initial focus on the gut microbiota to include microbial metabolism, epithelial barrier integrity, immune and endocrine signaling, and host-microbial interactions. This review uses a functional gut ecosystem framework to integrate these mechanisms and examine how diet and other exposures influence skeletal health.
RECENT FINDINGS: No consistent microbial signature of osteoporosis has emerged across populations or experimental models. Instead, recent studies indicate that skeletal responses are associated with functional outputs of the gut ecosystem, including nutrient bioavailability, microbial co-metabolic products, barrier integrity, and host sensing. Gut-derived signals may act directly on bone or be further processed by the host. Diverse interventions, including whole foods, probiotics, postbiotics, and targeted therapies, can converge on these functions. Bone responds to the integrated biological signals generated by the gut ecosystem rather than microbial composition alone. Defining these functions and individual responder phenotypes may provide new approaches for preserving skeletal health.

title: Root rot suppression by synthetic microbiota is associated with rhizosphere bacterial shifts and amino acid metabolism.
authors: Zhu Ning; Zhao Peijie; Liu Xinyi; Leng Feifan; Guo Xiaopeng et al.
abstract: Root rot caused by Fusarium oxysporum (F. oxysporum) severely constrains Codonopsis pilosula (C. pilosula) production. Indigenous culturable bacteria associated with C. pilosula were screened for antifungal activity, plant growth-promoting traits, and interstrain compatibility, and two defined three-member synthetic microbial communities, SCI and SCII, were constructed. Both SynComs alleviated root rot, with SCI showing stronger overall performance and a biocontrol efficacy of 57.8%, together with improved root growth and photosynthetic performance. Rhizosphere bacterial profiling was integrated with rhizosphere metabolite profiling and root tissue metabolomics. SynCom treatment was associated with limited changes in overall bacterial diversity but variation in specific rhizosphere taxa. In roots, pathway-enrichment patterns shifted from sulfur metabolism and oxidative stress-related processes under pathogen stress toward amino acid-related metabolism after SynCom treatment, accompanied by treatment-associated variation in medicinally relevant metabolite features. Associations between metabolic changes and potentially beneficial bacteria indicated coordinated variation between host metabolism and rhizosphere bacterial composition. In vitro assays further showed that L-valine elicited chemotactic and growth responses in a representative Sphingomonas isolate. Collectively, SynCom-mediated root rot suppression was associated with constituent-strain antagonism, plant recovery, rhizosphere bacterial shifts, and amino acid-related metabolic variation.

title: Cardiovascular resilience in centenarians.
authors: Carrera-Bastos Pedro; Plaza-Florido Abel; Pérez-Prieto Inmaculada; Radom-Aizik Shlomit; Franceschi Claudio et al.
abstract: Centenarians - individuals aged ≥100 years - provide a unique human model for understanding resilience to cardiovascular ageing. Although cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, including hypertension, heart failure, atrial fibrillation and chronic kidney disease, are common in centenarians, their onset is typically delayed relative to that in individuals aged 80-100 years. Centenarians characteristically have structural changes in the heart and vessels, including concentric left ventricular remodelling, increased myocardial stiffness and vascular ageing, but often without the expected burden of myocardial infarction or overt heart failure. Their cardiometabolic profile is generally favourable, marked by preserved insulin sensitivity in cohorts with a low prevalence of diabetes mellitus, mid-range lipid levels and a low prevalence of obesity. Centenarians also have a distinctive inflammatory and gastrointestinal phenotype, characterized by chronic low-grade inflammation with elevated anti-inflammatory signalling, a gut microbiome that more closely resembles that of younger adults, and preserved intestinal barrier integrity. Genetically and epigenetically, exceptional longevity reflects highly polygenic contributions, selective maintenance of genomic stability and markedly younger epigenetic age compared with chronological age. In this Review, we summarize data on the cardiovascular system among centenarians by framing observations of longevity as a composite of delayed pathology, adaptive compensation and survivorship selection. Understanding the biological, behavioural and environmental mechanisms underlying cardiovascular resilience in extreme longevity might inform strategies to extend cardiovascular healthspan across all ages.
